sources.title: Linked-list middle C++ fixture plus independent index oracle

claims.text: The source asks only how to locate a linked-list middle element using fast/slow pointers; API, empty/even/cycle semantics are not preserved source constraints.
Under the declared finite acyclic contract, each loop advances slow by one edge and fast by two, so termination leaves slow at index floor(n/2).
The executable fixture verifies nullptr for empty input, unique odd middle, second middle for even input under the explicit answer-side contract, large lengths and topology preservation.
The implementation advances pointers only forward a constant number of times per traversed node and stores only two local pointers, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for finite acyclic input.

validation.command: g++ writer fixture; independent Python step-count oracle

boundary_tests.expected: explicit answer-side contract returns second middle at index n/2

boundary_tests.actual: writer fixture snapshots all next pointers and passes

findings: The repository source preserves exactly one question asking how to locate the middle element of a linked list with fast/slow pointers; it does not specify API, empty-input behavior, even-length tie semantics or cyclic-input behavior.
The candidate explicitly labels finite acyclic singly-linked input, nullptr for empty input and second-middle behavior for even lengths as answer-side contracts instead of source facts.
The loop guard ensures fast->next exists before the two-step advance, so empty, single-node and short-list boundaries avoid invalid dereference.
The invariant is stated at the right level: fast advances twice as many edges as slow, and on termination slow has advanced floor(n/2) edges.
The standalone C++ fixture covers lengths 0..20 plus 999/1000/1001 and verifies every next pointer remains unchanged.
A separately authored step-count oracle checks every length from 0 through 10000 and independently confirms floor(n/2) slow steps.
The candidate does not fabricate project experience and explicitly warns that cyclic input breaks the tail-null termination premise.
